clue.text: Sporting legend no saint? That's about right

indicators.note: about means going round, so the phrase for a sinner surrounds the letter for right

parts.note: someone who is no saint is a bad man

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a sporting hero was a sinner and is told that is about right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's about' puts R inside BAD MAN. Don Bradman was the great Australian cricketer.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Donald Bradman, Australian batsman with a Test average near 100, is a cricketing legend.

clue.text: Organ stop not working? Keep hitting

indicators.note: not means the word for working is taken away

parts.note: a bombardon is a deep reed stop on an organ
on means working, as a machine is on

explanation.surface: An organist finds a stop broken and keeps thumping it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' removes ON from BOMBARDON.
explanation.definitionFit: To bombard is to attack continuously, as with shells or questions.

clue.text: Wind very light for VIP transport

parts.note: air is moving air, a wind
force one on the Beaufort scale is very light wind

explanation.surface: A breeze too gentle to carry an important person's transport.
explanation.walkthrough: The Beaufort scale grades wind from calm to hurricane; Force One is 'light air', barely moving.
explanation.definitionFit: Air Force One is the call sign of the aircraft carrying the US President.

clue.text: Small sheep, stupid, falling over

indicators.note: falling over means the whole run is upended and read backwards

parts.note: a teg is a sheep in its second year
dim means stupid

explanation.surface: A little sheep, rather dense, keeps tumbling over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'falling over' turns TEGDIM round. TEG is a two-year-old sheep.
explanation.definitionFit: Midget used as an adjective means very small, like a midget submarine.

clue.text: Last of a dozen irrepressibly talking?

definitions.text: Last of a dozen irrepressibly talking?

parts.words: Last of a dozen irrepressibly talking?
parts.note: plays on the idiom of chattering at a rate of nineteen to the dozen: in such a dozen the final one has that ordinal number

explanation.walkthrough: To talk 'nineteen to the dozen' is to chatter nonstop; if a dozen held nineteen, its last would be this one.
explanation.definitionFit: This ordinal comes after eighteenth, so it is the final item of a dozen counted by the chatterbox idiom.

clue.text: Foolish gentleman gets nothing to the boundaries, facing fast bowlers, say

indicators.note: say signals that the word for the bowlers is only pronounced, not spelt

parts.note: in cricket slang fast bowlers are quicks
O, the figure zero, means nothing

indicators.note: the boundaries of the words to the are their outermost letters, first and last

explanation.surface: A cricket picture: a silly man scores nothing at the boundary while facing the fast bowling.
explanation.walkthrough: QUIX sounds like QUICKS ('say'); 'facing' puts it before O, then 'boundaries' takes T and E, the first and last letters of 'to the'. Don Quixote is Cervantes's deluded knight.
explanation.definitionFit: Don Quixote, Cervantes's deluded knight who tilts at windmills, is the archetypal foolish gentleman.

clue.text: Court in sporty vehicle

definitions.meaning: a quadrangle, the courtyard of a college
a ... bike, a four-wheeled off-road motorbike

explanation.surface: A tennis court sits inside a sports car.
explanation.definitionFit: A quad is a college courtyard, and a quad bike is a sporty all-terrain machine.

clue.text: Wanted to know if Independent contained lots of pages

indicators.note: contained means the abbreviation for Independent holds the next piece

parts.note: a quire is a set of sheets of paper, about 24

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether the Independent newspaper ran to many pages.
explanation.walkthrough: IND holds QUIRE as IN...D. The Independent is a British newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: To inquire is to ask, so inquired is a straight synonym for wanted to know.

clue.text: Noisily finished eggs

indicators.note: noisily means the word is heard spoken rather than spelt

parts.note: over means finished

explanation.surface: Someone loudly polished off eggs.
explanation.walkthrough: In a non-rhotic British accent OVER sounds like OVA.
explanation.definitionFit: Ova is the plural of ovum, the Latin word for an egg cell.

clue.text: Having some spare time, read up in desert father

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the letters read from bottom to top, backwards
having some means only part of the words is taken, a run inside them

explanation.surface: With some free time, someone reads about one of the early Christian hermits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Having some' takes ETIMERE from 'spare time, read', and 'up' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: An eremite is a hermit, and the Desert Fathers were early Christian hermits in Egypt.

clue.text: Ruin good book, hiding the conclusion

indicators.note: hiding the conclusion means the final letter of the gospel's name is concealed and dropped

parts.note: Mark is a gospel, a book of the Good Book

explanation.surface: Someone spoils a fine novel by concealing how it ends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good book' is a gospel here, MARK, which loses its last letter K.
explanation.definitionFit: To mar something is to spoil or damage it, a straight synonym for ruin as a verb.

clue.text: Ballet step, as left in completed opera

indicators.note: in places the run of short pieces inside the word for completed

parts.note: something completed is done
a pas is a step in ballet
qua is Latin for as, in the capacity of

explanation.surface: A ballet step is left out of a finished opera production.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' splits the word for completed around the three short pieces. QUA, Latin for 'in the capacity of', is a crossword staple for 'as'.
explanation.definitionFit: Don Pasquale is a comic opera by Donizetti, first staged in 1843.

clue.text: It's Cupid to a T, helplessly entangling others

indicators.note: entangling means the jumbled letters wrap round the other piece, holding it inside
helplessly suggests letters thrown into disorder, so to a T is rearranged

parts.note: more can mean others, as in some more people

explanation.surface: A Cupid figure is described as exactly right, hopelessly tangling up other people in love.
explanation.walkthrough: 'helplessly' rearranges TOAT into A...TTO, which by 'entangling' holds MORE.
explanation.definitionFit: An amoretto is a small cupid, the winged infant of love often shown in Renaissance art.

clue.text: I run ahead to little Francesca's place

indicators.note: ahead tells us the letter for run stands in front of the letter I

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for run
mini means little

explanation.surface: Someone runs on ahead to the home of a girl called Francesca.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ahead' puts R before I. Francesca da Rimini is the tragic lover in Dante's Inferno, and Rimini is an Italian resort.
explanation.definitionFit: Francesca da Rimini, from Dante's Inferno, takes her name from the Italian town she came from.

clue.text: Contributing to line out, fit, but not for Sale

parts.note: someone contributing to a team or a band is in a team or in a band

indicators.note: out suggests the letters are put out of order, so line is rearranged

parts.note: able means fit, capable

explanation.surface: Someone helps at a rugby lineout, fit, though not on the transfer list at Sale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges LINE as LIEN. Sale is a rugby club near Manchester, which sets up the sporty surface and makes the capital fair.
explanation.definitionFit: Something inalienable cannot be transferred or sold away, such as an inalienable right.

clue.text: Sent choral arrangement for dance

indicators.note: an arrangement of music rearranges the letters of sent choral

explanation.surface: Someone sends off a choral piece arranged for dancing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arrangement' rearranges the letters of 'Sent choral'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Charleston is a lively 1920s dance named after the city in South Carolina.

clue.text: Get down, here

parts.note: reads as an order to drop low, and also as naming the bird from which soft feathers are gathered

explanation.walkthrough: To duck is to get down; and a duck, like the eider, is where down comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb this word means to stoop quickly; as a noun it names the waterfowl whose fluffy feathers fill pillows.

clue.text: Persuade husband to see about chap for garden

parts.note: to get someone to do something is to persuade them

indicators.note: about means the word for see goes round the word for chap

parts.note: taken as written
a man is a chap

explanation.surface: Someone is urged to get their husband to visit a fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Persuade' is a verb here: to get someone to do something. The 'about' container sits inside the end of the charade, not around all of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Gethsemane is the garden on the Mount of Olives where Jesus prayed before his arrest.

clue.text: Plain fare in cooker, so eat out

parts.note: a pot is a vessel for cooking

indicators.note: out means the letters are jumbled, so so eat is rearranged

explanation.surface: Simple food sits in the cooker, so eat out instead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges SOEAT to ATOES.
explanation.definitionFit: Potatoes are basic everyday food, the classic plain fare.

clue.text: Coastal feature on right, after walk

indicators.note: after says the pieces for on and right follow the word for walk

parts.note: a prom is a promenade, a seaside walk
taken as written
Tory means right-wing, the political right

explanation.surface: A coastal landmark lies on the right after a seafront stroll.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' is taken literally, not as a link word. A prom is a British seafront promenade; Tory means the political right.
explanation.definitionFit: A promontory is a headland, a high point of land jutting out into the sea.

clue.text: Begged to go round island: so queue, perhaps

indicators.note: to go round means the word for begged is set around the island

parts.note: pled is a form of pleaded, begged
an ait is a small river island

explanation.surface: Someone begs to tour an island and is told to form a queue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to go round' is the container signal. In the old sense a queue is a pigtail, i.e. plaited hair; an ait (or eyot) is a small island in a river.
explanation.definitionFit: A queue in the old sense is a pigtail, which is plaited hair, hence an example of something plaited.

clue.text: Well-established tree at back of arboretum

parts.note: a fir is a kind of tree

indicators.note: at back of picks out the final letter of arboretum

explanation.surface: A long-standing tree grows at the back of an arboretum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at back of' gives M, the last letter of 'arboretum'.
explanation.definitionFit: Firm means securely fixed or established, as in a firm friendship.

clue.text: Madonna holding Child, solid work

indicators.note: holding means the name of the Madonna goes round the word for child

parts.note: the Madonna is the Virgin Mary
a son is a child

explanation.surface: A picture of the Madonna with the infant in her arms, a solid piece of work.
explanation.walkthrough: MARY holds SON as MA...RY.
explanation.definitionFit: Masonry is stonework, building with stone or brick, a solid kind of work.

clue.text: One seen around Cambridge embracing loose blonde

indicators.note: embracing means the area round Cambridge surrounds the word for loose

parts.note: the Fens are marshy flatlands around Cambridge
lax means loose

explanation.surface: Someone spotted near Cambridge hugs a careless fair-haired person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'embracing' is the container signal. The Fens are low-lying marshland in eastern England around Cambridge.
explanation.definitionFit: Flaxen means pale yellow like flax fibre, describing blonde hair.

clue.text: Call aide about missing link

indicators.note: about means turning round, so the pair of words is read backwards

parts.note: to name is to call
a PA is a personal assistant, an aide

explanation.surface: A request to ring an assistant concerning some missing connection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' turns NAMEPA backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: An ape-man was the supposed missing link between apes and humans in old evolutionary theory.

clue.text: Senilely confused straight paths

indicators.note: confused suggests muddled letters, so senilely is rearranged

explanation.surface: An old person's muddled mind is pictured following straight paths.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confused' rearranges the letters of 'Senilely'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ley lines are supposed straight alignments linking ancient sites across the landscape.

clue.text: Write to new founder of colony

parts.note: to pen is to write

explanation.surface: Someone writes to the newcomer who founded a colony.
explanation.definitionFit: William Penn founded the American colony of Pennsylvania in 1681.

clue.text: Go public with short cut for VAT, say

parts.note: a go is a turn
overt means open, public

indicators.note: short means a word lacking its final letter

parts.note: to axe is to cut

explanation.surface: A business goes public along with a quick trim to its value added tax.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' takes the last letter E off AXE. VAT is value added tax, Britain's sales tax.
explanation.definitionFit: VAT is an example of a tax levied on turnover, the sales a business makes.

clue.text: A few yards travelled, stopping short

indicators.note: stopping short means the word ends early, its final letter lost

parts.note: rode means travelled, as on horseback

explanation.surface: Someone covered a few yards and then stopped suddenly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stopping short' cuts E from RODE.
explanation.definitionFit: A rod is an old measure of length, five and a half yards.

clue.text: Writer returned to store

indicators.note: returned means read back, so the pen point is turned round

parts.note: a nib is the writing point of a pen

explanation.surface: An author returns to a shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned' turns NIB round.
explanation.definitionFit: To bin is to put away for keeping, as wine is binned in a cellar, so it can mean to store.

clue.text: Almost avoid boy — he liked little girls

indicators.note: almost means not quite complete, so the last letter goes

parts.note: to dodge is to avoid
a son is a boy

explanation.surface: Someone nearly avoids a lad, a man fond of young girls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' drops the last letter E of DODGE.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Dodgson, writing as Lewis Carroll, was famously devoted to child friends such as Alice Liddell.

clue.text: In city, messenger heading off for sisters' place

indicators.note: In places the shortened messenger inside the city's abbreviation

parts.note: NY is New York

indicators.note: heading off means the first letter is cut away

parts.note: a runner carries messages

explanation.surface: A city courier sets off for the sisters' place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heading off' drops the first letter of the messenger word, and 'In' puts what is left inside New York's abbreviation, which is split as N...Y.
explanation.definitionFit: A nunnery is a convent, home to a community of religious sisters.
